mcqs.question: Why does PCA choose the direction of maximum variance as its first principal component?
options: Because high-variance directions are always the least noisy
Because it's the fastest direction to compute
Because a direction where points spread out the most carries the most information for telling points apart
Because it always aligns with one of the original features
mcqs.explanation: A direction where every point looks nearly the same tells you nothing useful; a direction with wide spread is where points genuinely differ, which is why PCA treats variance as a proxy for information. It's not the fastest to compute, doesn't guarantee low noise, and rarely aligns with a single original feature.

mcqs.question: In PCA, what does an eigenvalue tell you about its corresponding eigenvector (principal component)?
options: How correlated that component is with the target label
How much variance in the data lies along that component's direction
The number of original features that make up that component
Whether that component should be standardized before use
mcqs.explanation: The eigenvalue is the amount of variance captured along its eigenvector's direction — that's exactly why sorting by eigenvalue ranks the components from most to least informative. PCA is unsupervised, so it has no concept of a target label to correlate with.

mcqs.question: You run PCA on raw, unstandardized features where income is in the tens of thousands and age is in single/double digits. What's the likely result?
options: PCA automatically rescales internally, so there is no issue
The first principal component will be dominated by income purely due to its larger numeric scale
PCA will fail to run entirely
Age will dominate because PCA favors integer-valued features
mcqs.explanation: PCA chases variance, and variance scales with the units a feature is measured in — so an unscaled, large-magnitude feature like income will swamp the components regardless of whether it's actually more informative. PCA does not auto-standardize, and it won't fail to run; it will just produce a misleading result.
